## Proof

Let $P:SO(n)\to SO(n)$ be the squaring map $P(A)=A^{2}$. We determine for which $n$ the differential $dP_{A}$ fails to be a linear isomorphism at some $A\in SO(n)$.

**Step 1. Compute the differential.** For $H\in T_{A}SO(n)$,
$$P(A+tH)=(A+tH)^{2}=A^{2}+t(AH+HA)+O(t^{2}),$$
so $dP_{A}(H)=AH+HA$. Since $T_{A}SO(n)=\{AX:X\in\mathfrak{so}(n)\}$, write $H=AX$ with $X$ skew-symmetric. Then
$$dP_{A}(AX)=A^{2}X+AXA=A^{2}\bigl(X+A^{-1}XA\bigr).$$
Since left-multiplication by $A^{2}$ is a linear isomorphism $T_{I}SO(n)\to T_{A^{2}}SO(n)$, the map $dP_{A}$ is an isomorphism iff the linear map
$$L_{A}:\mathfrak{so}(n)\to\mathfrak{so}(n),\qquad L_{A}(X)=X+A^{-1}XA$$
is invertible. (One checks $A^{-1}XA$ is skew, so $L_{A}$ is well-defined and lands in $\mathfrak{so}(n)$.)

**Step 2. Eigenvalues of the Adjoint term.** The map $X\mapsto A^{-1}XA=\operatorname{Ad}(A^{-1})(X)$ is the adjoint action. Under the standard identification $\mathfrak{so}(n)\cong\Lambda^{2}\mathbb{R}^{n}$, $\operatorname{Ad}(A^{-1})$ corresponds to $\Lambda^{2}(A^{-1})$. Hence if $\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{n}$ are the complex eigenvalues of $A$, the eigenvalues of $\operatorname{Ad}(A^{-1})$ on $\mathfrak{so}(n)$ are
$$\lambda_{a}^{-1}\lambda_{b}^{-1},\qquad 1\le a<b\le n.$$
Therefore the eigenvalues of $L_{A}=I+\operatorname{Ad}(A^{-1})$ are $1+\lambda_{a}^{-1}\lambda_{b}^{-1}$, and
$$L_{A}\text{ is singular}\iff \exists\,a<b:\ \lambda_{a}^{-1}\lambda_{b}^{-1}=-1\iff \exists\,a<b:\ \lambda_{a}\lambda_{b}=-1.$$

**Step 3. Eigenvalue structure of $A\in SO(n)$.** Over $\mathbb{C}$, $A$ is conjugate to a block-diagonal matrix with $2\times2$ rotation blocks $R(\theta_{j})$ (eigenvalues $e^{\pm i\theta_{j}}$, $\theta_{j}\in[0,\pi]$) and, when $n$ is odd, a single $1\times1$ block $[1]$. Thus the eigenvalue multiset is
$$\{e^{\pm i\theta_{1}},\dots,e^{\pm i\theta_{m}}\}\quad(n=2m),\qquad \{1,e^{\pm i\theta_{1}},\dots,e^{\pm i\theta_{m}}\}\quad(n=2m+1).$$

**Step 4. Determine when a pair has product $-1$.**

- *Within a conjugate pair* $\{e^{i\theta},e^{-i\theta}\}$: the product is $e^{i\theta}e^{-i\theta}=1\neq-1$. So a single rotation block alone never causes singularity.
- *Lone $1$ paired with $e^{\pm i\theta}$*: product $e^{\pm i\theta}=-1\iff\theta=\pi$. Requires $n$ odd and a $\pi$-rotation block.
- *Two blocks* $e^{\pm i\theta_{a}}\cdot e^{\pm i\theta_{b}}=-1\iff \theta_{a}\pm\theta_{b}\equiv\pi\pmod{2\pi}$, in particular $\theta_{a}+\theta_{b}=\pi$ (e.g. $\theta_{a}=\theta_{b}=\pi/2$, or $\theta_{a}=0,\theta_{b}=\pi$). Requires at least two rotation blocks (i.e. $n\ge4$), or one block plus the lone $1$ with $\theta=\pi$ (i.e. $n\ge3$ odd).

**Step 5. Enumerate by $n$.**

- $n=1$: $SO(1)=\{I\}$; $\mathfrak{so}(1)=0$. $dP$ is the trivial isomorphism of a $0$-dimensional space. **Isomorphism.**
- $n=2$: $SO(2)$ is abelian, so $A^{-1}XA=X$ for all $A$, giving $L_{A}=2I$, always invertible. Equivalently the only eigenvalue pair is the conjugate pair with product $1$. **Isomorphism everywhere.**
- $n=3$: take $A=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1)\in SO(3)$ (rotation by $\pi$). Eigenvalues $1,-1,-1$; the pair $(1,-1)$ has product $-1$. Concretely, $\mathfrak{so}(3)\cong\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and $\operatorname{Ad}(A)$ acts as $\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1)$, so $L_{A}=I+\operatorname{Ad}(A)$ has eigenvalues $2,0,0$. **Not an isomorphism.**
- $n\ge4$ even: take two rotation blocks with $\theta_{1}=\theta_{2}=\pi/2$ (eigenvalues $i,-i,i,-i,\dots$); the pair $(i,i)$ has product $-1$. **Not an isomorphism.**
- $n\ge5$ odd: take one block with $\theta_{1}=\pi$ (eigenvalues $-1,-1$) together with the lone eigenvalue $1$; the pair $(1,-1)$ has product $-1$. **Not an isomorphism.**

**Conclusion.** The differential $dP$ fails to be an isomorphism (at some point of $SO(n)$) exactly for
$$\boxed{\,n\ge 3\,}.$$
For $n=1,2$ the differential $dP_{A}=2\,\mathrm{id}$ (up to the canonical identifications) is an isomorphism at every $A$; for every $n\ge3$ there exists $A\in SO(n)$ possessing two eigenvalues whose product is $-1$, which makes $L_{A}$—and hence $dP_{A}$—singular.

## Proof

Let $P:SO(n)\to SO(n)$ be the squaring map $P(A)=A^{2}$. We determine for which $n$ the differential $dP_{A}$ fails to be a linear isomorphism at some $A\in SO(n)$.

**Step 1. Compute the differential.** For $H\in T_{A}SO(n)$,
$$P(A+tH)=(A+tH)^{2}=A^{2}+t(AH+HA)+O(t^{2}),$$
so $dP_{A}(H)=AH+HA$. Since $T_{A}SO(n)=\{AX:X\in\mathfrak{so}(n)\}$, write $H=AX$ with $X$ skew-symmetric. Then
$$dP_{A}(AX)=A^{2}X+AXA=A^{2}\bigl(X+A^{-1}XA\bigr).$$
Since left-multiplication by $A^{2}$ is a linear isomorphism $T_{I}SO(n)\to T_{A^{2}}SO(n)$, the map $dP_{A}$ is an isomorphism iff the linear map
$$L_{A}:\mathfrak{so}(n)\to\mathfrak{so}(n),\qquad L_{A}(X)=X+A^{-1}XA$$
is invertible. (One checks $A^{-1}XA$ is skew, so $L_{A}$ is well-defined and lands in $\mathfrak{so}(n)$.)

**Step 2. Eigenvalues of the Adjoint term.** The map $X\mapsto A^{-1}XA=\operatorname{Ad}(A^{-1})(X)$ is the adjoint action. Under the standard identification $\mathfrak{so}(n)\cong\Lambda^{2}\mathbb{R}^{n}$, $\operatorname{Ad}(A^{-1})$ corresponds to $\Lambda^{2}(A^{-1})$. Hence if $\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{n}$ are the complex eigenvalues of $A$, the eigenvalues of $\operatorname{Ad}(A^{-1})$ on $\mathfrak{so}(n)$ are
$$\lambda_{a}^{-1}\lambda_{b}^{-1},\qquad 1\le a<b\le n.$$
Therefore the eigenvalues of $L_{A}=I+\operatorname{Ad}(A^{-1})$ are $1+\lambda_{a}^{-1}\lambda_{b}^{-1}$, and
$$L_{A}\text{ is singular}\iff \exists\,a<b:\ \lambda_{a}^{-1}\lambda_{b}^{-1}=-1\iff \exists\,a<b:\ \lambda_{a}\lambda_{b}=-1.$$

**Step 3. Eigenvalue structure of $A\in SO(n)$.** Over $\mathbb{C}$, $A$ is conjugate to a block-diagonal matrix with $2\times2$ rotation blocks $R(\theta_{j})$ (eigenvalues $e^{\pm i\theta_{j}}$, $\theta_{j}\in[0,\pi]$) and, when $n$ is odd, a single $1\times1$ block $[1]$. Thus the eigenvalue multiset is
$$\{e^{\pm i\theta_{1}},\dots,e^{\pm i\theta_{m}}\}\quad(n=2m),\qquad \{1,e^{\pm i\theta_{1}},\dots,e^{\pm i\theta_{m}}\}\quad(n=2m+1).$$

**Step 4. Determine when a pair has product $-1$.**

- *Within a conjugate pair* $\{e^{i\theta},e^{-i\theta}\}$: the product is $e^{i\theta}e^{-i\theta}=1\neq-1$. So a single rotation block alone never causes singularity.
- *Lone $1$ paired with $e^{\pm i\theta}$*: product $e^{\pm i\theta}=-1\iff\theta=\pi$. Requires $n$ odd and a $\pi$-rotation block.
- *Two blocks* $e^{\pm i\theta_{a}}\cdot e^{\pm i\theta_{b}}=-1\iff \theta_{a}\pm\theta_{b}\equiv\pi\pmod{2\pi}$, in particular $\theta_{a}+\theta_{b}=\pi$ (e.g. $\theta_{a}=\theta_{b}=\pi/2$, or $\theta_{a}=0,\theta_{b}=\pi$). Requires at least two rotation blocks (i.e. $n\ge4$), or one block plus the lone $1$ with $\theta=\pi$ (i.e. $n\ge3$ odd).

**Step 5. Enumerate by $n$.**

- $n=1$: $SO(1)=\{I\}$; $\mathfrak{so}(1)=0$. $dP$ is the trivial isomorphism of a $0$-dimensional space. **Isomorphism.**
- $n=2$: $SO(2)$ is abelian, so $A^{-1}XA=X$ for all $A$, giving $L_{A}=2I$, always invertible. Equivalently the only eigenvalue pair is the conjugate pair with product $1$. **Isomorphism everywhere.**
- $n=3$: take $A=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1)\in SO(3)$ (rotation by $\pi$). Eigenvalues $1,-1,-1$; the pair $(1,-1)$ has product $-1$. Concretely, $\mathfrak{so}(3)\cong\mathbb{R}^{3}$ and $\operatorname{Ad}(A)$ acts as $\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1)$, so $L_{A}=I+\operatorname{Ad}(A)$ has eigenvalues $2,0,0$. **Not an isomorphism.**
- $n\ge4$ even: take two rotation blocks with $\theta_{1}=\theta_{2}=\pi/2$ (eigenvalues $i,-i,i,-i,\dots$); the pair $(i,i)$ has product $-1$. **Not an isomorphism.**
- $n\ge5$ odd: take one block with $\theta_{1}=\pi$ (eigenvalues $-1,-1$) together with the lone eigenvalue $1$; the pair $(1,-1)$ has product $-1$. **Not an isomorphism.**

**Conclusion.** The differential $dP$ fails to be an isomorphism (at some point of $SO(n)$) exactly for
$$\boxed{\,n\ge 3\,}.$$
For $n=1,2$ the differential $dP_{A}=2\,\mathrm{id}$ (up to the canonical identifications) is an isomorphism at every $A$; for every $n\ge3$ there exists $A\in SO(n)$ possessing two eigenvalues whose product is $-1$, which makes $L_{A}$—and hence $dP_{A}$—singular.
